title: Breast Cancer Classification in R
text:
This blog uses the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Original) from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0), loaded through the mlbench R package. Each row is a tumor sample score from 1 to 10 on nine cell characteristics.

library(mlbench)
library(ggplot2)

title: Breast Cancer Classification in R
text:
What I Did
I start by loading the data and converting the cell size score to a number. mlbench stores the scores as factors, which R treats as categories rather than values.

data(BreastCancer)
bc <- BreastCancer
# Scores are stored as factors; convert via character to get the real
# values (as.numeric on a factor alone returns level positions).
bc$Cell.size <- as.numeric(as.character(bc$Cell.size))
head(bc)

2 1002945            5         4          4             5            7
3 1015425            3         1          1             1            2
4 1016277            6         8          8             1            3
5 1017023            4         1          1             3            2
6 1017122            8        10         10             8            7
  Bare.nuclei Bl.cromatin Normal.nucleoli Mitoses     Class
1           1           3               1       1    benign
2          10           3               2       1    benign
3           2           3               1       1    benign
4           4           3               7       1    benign
5           1           3               1       1    benign
6          10           9               7       1 malignant


First, I count the samples in each group and compare their average cell size score.

table(bc$Class)


   benign malignant 
      458       241 

aggregate(Cell.size ~ Class, data = bc, FUN = mean)

      Class Cell.size
1    benign  1.325328
2 malignant  6.572614


Next, I plot the distribution of cell size score for each diagnosis. Each box covers the middle 50% of samples, with a line at the median.

ggplot(bc, aes(x = Class, y = Cell.size, fill = Class)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Cell size score by diagnosis",
    x = "Diagnosis",
    y = "Uniformity of cell size (1–10)"
  )







Figure 1: Distribution of Cell Size Uniformity Score by Diagnosis.

title: Breast Cancer Classification in R
text:
What I Found
The dataset contains 458 benign and 241 malignant samples. Malignant samples have an average cell size score of about 6.6, compared with about 1.3 for benign samples. Most benign samples score exactly 1, so their box collapses into a flat line, with the less common higher scores shown as individual points. The boxplot shows the same pattern: the malignant box sits well above the benign one. This suggests cell size uniformity is a strong indicator of diagnosis, though not a perfect separator, since some malignant samples still score low.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day in beautiful Vancouver.


Week 1 ✅
My first day of orientation was a whirlwind of both excitement and nervousness. Sitting down at my assigned table, I found myself between two people who’d previously worked as software engineers — and immediately felt like a small fish in a very big pond. Between program deliverables, course schedules, and constant reminders about how fast-paced this program is, I could feel the gears in my mind working overtime just to keep up.
The first week of classes didn’t slow things down much. DSCI 523 (R Programming) and DSCI 511 (Python Programming) felt manageable, but I hit a wall with the statistics and GitHub components of 521 — the last time I’d properly touched statistics was AP Stats my senior year of high school, back in 2018. I’ve since learned that undergrad biostatistics from six years ago doesn’t count for as much as I’d hoped.
What surprised me most wasn’t the workload itself, but how fast my confidence eroded once I actually sat down to do the work — labs and worksheets that felt straightforward in lecture took me right up to the deadline. Between the pace and the constant reminders to also rest and take care of myself, week one has been a genuine exercise in learning to stay afloat.

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

title: Breast Cancer Classification in Python
text:
What I Did
Let’s take a look at our data by loading the dataset through scikit-learn’s load_breast_cancer(). Each row is a tumor sample described by measurements of its cell nuclei. I load the data into a pandas DataFrame and label each sample as malignant or benign.

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
# rename to df for easier referencing
df = bc.frame
# 'target' is the diagnosis of each sample, 1 for benign and 0 for malignant
# We pair each name with its position using enumerate(), turn the pairs 
# into a lookup table with dict(), then use map() to replace each value.
df["diagnosis"] = df["target"].map(dict(enumerate(bc.target_names)))

First, I count the samples in each group and compare their average nucleus radius.

title: Breast Cancer Classification in Python
text:
What I Found
The dataset contains 357 benign and 212 malignant samples. Malignant samples have a mean radius of about 17, compared with about 12 benign samples. The boxplot shows the same pattern: the malignant box sits clearly above the benign one, with only a little overlap. This suggests nucleus size is a strong indicator of diagnosis, although not a perfect correlation, since some samples fall in the range where the two groups overlap.

title: About
text:
Prior to the MDS program, I pursued a career in veterinary science — working as a dog-walker, pet-sitter, animal-welfare officer at the SPCA, then as a veterinary assistant at the Bureau Veterinaire Express in Montreal and Main Street Animal Hospital in North Vancouver. In undergrad, my first biostatistics course gave me my first real experience with R — and with it, a piqued interest in data science. My time in animal healthcare had already exposed me to the messy, high-stakes data that healthcare and life sciences generate, so after graduation I worked briefly as a Data Annotator for Outlier AI and completed the Google Data Analytics Certificate, two experiences that solidified my decision to pursue data science as a career.
I don’t come from a traditional tech background, but I’ve come to see data science as one of the clearest paths to real impact in healthcare — using data to catch patterns earlier, personalize treatment, and make better decisions faster. Through UBC’s MDS program, I’m looking forward to building a rigorous foundation in machine learning, statistical modeling, neural networks, and probability theory. Longer-term, I hope to work at the intersection of data science and healthcare, building predictive models for precision medicine and disease analytics.
Outside the roadmap to becoming a Data Scientist, I enjoy a myriad of hobbies. My longest-standing love is playing tennis, which I’ve played for over 10 years now. My love language is making food for my family and friends, since baking for myself always feels more self-serving. Reading is one of my favorite pastimes (when I find the time!); I’m drawn to literary fiction that explores identity and isolation, and I’m currently reading “The Goldfinch” by Donna Tartt.
